newsitem.title: USA: Corn prices soar, coffee falls, gasoline up.
newsitem.headline: Corn prices soar, coffee falls, gasoline up.

text.p: Corn prices soared on Tuesday after the U.S. Agriculture Department cut nearly a half-billion bushels off its estimate of this year's crop after taking its first field surveys.

In other markets, cotton prices also rose on a cut on government crop estimates. Wheat fell but soybeans rose despite estimates for bigger crops this year. Coffee fell on easing supply worries, while gasoline soared as traders speculated that supplies fell last week.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn futures shot up the 12-cent-a-bushel daily trading limit at the opening bell. Corn for delivery in December closed the 12-cent limit higher at $2.65-1/4.

Triggering the rally was the Agriculture Department's estimate of corn production at 9.276 billion bushels, sharply below the forecast of 9.70 billion bushels in July and below an average of analysts' estimate of 9.55 billion bushels.
"Hot and dry weather conditions have reduced the yield on dryland corn," the department said.
The production estimates were for conditions as of August 1. Scattered rains since that date in some Midwestern fields have eased moisture stress and aided corn growth.

But the sharp cut in the official government estimate, coming on the heels of crop stress reported in some Midwest corn areas in weekly state reports issued late on Monday, was too much buying incentive for speculators to ignore.
"Clearly the influence in corn was the crop report being much lower than expected and on top of that the decline in crop conditions," said Dale Gustafson, an analyst with Smith Barney.
"We'll probably be limit-up tomorrow, and maybe Thursday the market will get to where it wants to go," he said.

Floor traders in the corn pit reported unfilled buying orders in corn futures of roughly 110 million bushels, with 75 million bushels of buying orders alone in the December contract waiting to be filled.
Prices will expand to an 18-cent per bushel daily limit on Wednesday.
The strength in corn, the largest U.S. crop, spilled over to soybeans. Soybeans for September delivery closed 4-3/4 cents a bushel higher at $6.47-3/4.

That gain came despite the Agriculture Department's estimate for record soybean production of 2.744 billion bushels this year, up 15 percent from last year's crop and higher than trade expectations for 2.607 to 2.731 billion.
"With corn at the limit, it has spurred additional interest in the bean market from the speculative community," said Mark Widener, an analyst with Cargill Investor Services.
"But the trade realizes that the rains of the past 24 to 48 hours can help us achieve those record yields," he said.
Rain in the U.S. Midwest since Sunday is seen giving the developing soybean crop a big production boost, traders said.

Wheat prices closed lower after the government raised its estimate of this year's wheat crops to 2.531 billion bushels, above its July forecast of 2.431 billion and the average analysts' estimate for 2.476 billion.
September wheat closed down 2-3/4 cents a bushel at $3.61.

At the New York Cotton Exchange, December cotton closed 1.02 cents a pound higher at 74.78 cents. The Agriculture Department trimmed its estimate of this year's cotton crop to 17.8 million 480-pound bales from 18.0 million in July.
Coffee prices closed sharply lower as speculators sold contracts on easing worries about tight supplies as talk circulated of African and other coffees being shipped in.

Coffee for September delivery at the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York tumbled 11.15 cents a pound to close at 188.20 cents. The difference or spread with the December contract also narrowed, with December ending down 6.25 cents at 168.50.

"Prices are so inverted it is drawing coffee to the market," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "But keep in mind that much of the coffee graded is from Burundi, Peru or India and is not the highest quality."

Oil prices closed higher led by gasoline as traders speculated that the American Petroleum Institute in its weekly report on Tuesday evening would show a drop in gasoline stocks of one to three million barrels.

September gasoline settled 2.24 cents a gallon higher at 63.71 cents a gallon. Following gasoline, September crude oil finished 30 cents a barrel up at $19.99 while September heating oil ended 0.74 cent up at 55.10 cents a gallon.

After the close of day trading, the API reported that gasoline stocks fell only 863,000 barrels in the week ended August 8. Crude oil stocks rose 2.75 million barrels, versus expectations for a drop of one to three million barrels.
